analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace safety law to government workers and raises penalties for employers whose violations kill or injure workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee in May 2005, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strengthen the Occupational Safety and Health Act in several ways. It would extend OSHA protections to federal, state, and local government employees, who are currently largely outside the law. It would raise fines for safety violations, make it a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison to willfully violate safety rules in a way that kills a worker, strengthen protections for workers who report unsafe conditions, and require employers to provide safety gear like gloves and respirators at no cost to workers.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are workers in dangerous jobs: government employees who would gain OSHA coverage for the first time, and workers at private employers who would gain stronger fines, criminal accountability, faster whistleblower remedies, and free protective equipment. Families of workers killed on the job would gain new rights to see investigation reports and object to settlements that weaken citations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Government workers and employees in dangerous jobs

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA coverage to federal, state, and local government employees, who the 1970 law excluded, so public-sector workers would gain the same safety standards and enforcement as private-sector workers.

Raises civil penalties: the maximum for a willful violation goes from $70,000 to $100,000, and a serious violation that causes a worker's death could carry a fine of up to $250,000, with penalty amounts adjusted for inflation every four years.

Increases criminal penalties dramatically: a willful violation that causes a worker's death would carry up to 10 years in prison instead of the current 6 months, and a new crime covers willful violations causing serious bodily injury, punishable by up to 5 years.

Strengthens whistleblower protections: workers who report injuries or unsafe conditions could file complaints within 180 days, with a binding investigation timeline, reinstatement, back pay, and compensatory damages for those retaliated against.

Requires employers to provide personal protective equipment at no cost to employees, and directs the Labor Secretary to investigate every workplace death and every incident hospitalizing two or more workers.

Gives injured workers and families of killed workers new 'victims' rights': meetings with investigators, free copies of citations and reports, and a chance to object before the government withdraws or reduces a citation in a settlement.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: businesses and government agencies would pay higher fines when they violate safety rules, would have to buy and provide protective equipment rather than charging workers, and owners and managers would face much longer prison terms for willful violations that kill or seriously injure workers.

drawbacks.text: Higher fines and equipment costs raise compliance expenses for employers, and the heaviest burdens can fall on small businesses that lack in-house safety departments, though the equipment rule simply shifts a cost workers currently absorb themselves.

The criminal penalty increase is severe: a safety violation judged willful that results in death could mean a decade in prison, which critics of strict criminal liability argue can punish negligence and ordinary management decisions as if they were crimes.

Extending OSHA to state and local government employees raises costs for taxpayers in states that currently run their own public-sector safety programs, although the bill lets the Labor Secretary cede jurisdiction to other federal agencies with equally effective rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and targeted at a real gap: government workers have no general OSHA coverage, and the current maximum prison term for a willful violation that kills a worker is six months, one of the weakest penalties in federal law. The costs fall on employers, and the strongest objection is the severity of the new criminal penalties. On balance the bill is a straightforward pro-worker safety measure whose main design risk is over-criminalization, not harm to workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the bill on April 28, 2005, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Reps. George Miller, Robert Andrews, Stephen Lynch, Rosa DeLauro, and Michael Michaud.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and on May 20, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.

No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee and full committee never reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor or the Senate before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced higher fines, free-equipment mandates, and criminal exposure for safety violations are better off because the bill died without a vote; the government workers who would have gained OSHA coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided higher safety penalties

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were House Democrats, and with the Republican majority controlling the committee agenda, the bill got no action in the 109th Congress.

industries.industry: Private employers subject to OSHA (construction, manufacturing, and other high-hazard industries)
industries.note: The bill would have raised their fines, forced them to pay for workers' protective equipment, exposed them to longer prison terms for willful violations, and constrained their ability to negotiate down citations. What costs them is compliance with safety rules that protect their employees.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local government agencies as employers
industries.note: Public agencies would have been brought under OSHA for the first time, taking on new enforcement exposure and safety compliance costs for police, sanitation, corrections, and other public employees.
